pageSubline: Statistical analysis of Mexican federal procurement contracts

evolution.title: Model Evolution
evolution.subtitle: From expert-weighted checklist (v3.3) to the active model, v0.9.2, which only looks at each vendor’s past.

steps.v33Desc: 8 expert-weighted factors, IMF CRI aligned. AUC barely above random.
steps.v40Desc: Z-score normalization, Bayesian calibration, 9 corruption cases, 12 features.
steps.v50Desc: 12 sector sub-models, 15 documented cases, temporal train/test split.
steps.v51Desc: 22 cases including SAT EFOS Case 22: 38 RFC-confirmed ghost companies.
steps.v60Desc: ~748 cases, ~603 vendors. Vendor-stratified split (no vendor in both train+test), time-windowed labels, Optuna TPE.
steps.v52Desc: SHAP per-vendor explanations (456K vendors) + PyOD cross-model ensemble (9.3M scores) + KS drift monitoring. See Vendor Profile → Risk tab, Contract detail → AI-flagged, Dashboard → Cross-Model.
steps.v85Desc: Trained on the case set as of May 2026. One global ElasticNet, 18 active features, c_pu=0.32. HR=11.0%. Its stored test AUC could not be reproduced; on vendors linked after training it scored 0.656. Superseded on October 13, 2026 by v0.9.1; its scores are kept for rollback. Run: CAL-v8-202605020212.
steps.v91Desc: Retrained on the cleaned case set (October 2026; cases on record at training: {{atTraining}}; today: {{today}}). One global ElasticNet, 27 features (21 carry weight), c_pu=0.439. It published AUC 0.852 on 106 held-out vendors, but several features used years after the contract: a pre-registered test showed that edge was future information. Replaced by v0.9.2 in October 2026. Run: CAL-v91-202610131004.
steps.v91Title: Retrained on the cleaned case set
steps.v92Desc: v0.9.1’s recipe (same hyperparameters and labelling) over 17 features: each vendor’s history looks only at years before the contract; comparisons with its sector use the last three years, leaving the contract itself out. Chosen by a rule signed before the test (pre-registration 2, 22 October 2026). Forward-chained AUC 0.827 (95% CI 0.763 to 0.883); at equal vendor size 0.741. c_pu=0.436, HR about 10%. Also scores ComprasMX.

overview.p1End: . In the v0.9.2 model, each vendor’s history looks only at years before the contract; comparisons with its sector use the last three years, leaving the contract itself out. Tested forward (trained on earlier years and scored on the next, 2019 to 2025, vendor by vendor and year by year), it scores AUC 0.827 (95% CI 0.763 to 0.883). A score of 0.35 means this contract’s procurement characteristics resemble those of contracts in labelled cases; it is not a probability of corruption.
overview.pTriage: Read the score as a triage tool. It orders contracts within a sector and year by how closely they resemble contracts linked to documented cases. In years it did not see in training, it ranks a vendor with a case above one without about eight times in ten (AUC 0.83). Use it to decide what to read first, never to conclude anything about a company.
overview.pSizeBaseline: Vendor size carries much of that signal. On the same forward test, ranking only by the money a vendor had won in earlier years scores 0.790, against the model’s 0.827. At equal vendor size the model scores 0.741: a high score on a large supplier says something, but not much, beyond its size.
overview.formulaDescStart: Where z = z-score features, beta = learned coefficients, sigma = logistic sigmoid, c = PU correction (0.436). S(z) is a
overview.formulaDescEnd: — it measures how closely a contract's procurement characteristics resemble those of vendors later linked to documented cases. The score is a pattern-similarity signal, not a corruption probability estimate.
overview.highRiskSummaryEnd: (critical + high). The intercept is set so that 10% of scored contracts reach high or above, inside RUBLI’s own 2–15% calibration target. v0.9.2 is the active model (October 2026). One adjustment is made after scoring, for display only: above 0.60 the score is compressed so that it rises ever more slowly and tops out just below 0.95. Without it, some 89,000 contracts sat tied at exactly 1.00, which hid their order and read like certainty. No contract changes level, so the high-risk rate is the same; read 0.95 as “top of critical”, not as a probability. The uncompressed model score is kept in the data for reproducibility.
overview.tableFootnote: * Scored contracts only: the few contracts without a sector assignment are excluded from scoring.

features.p1: Each contract is described by 17 features, all measured as of the contract: vendor history uses only years before it, and sector baselines use the last three years, leaving the contract itself out. Ten are behavioural z-scores (amounts, concentration, network, procedure), one is recency, three compare the contract with others under the same budget line (partida), and three describe the vendor's earlier history: how many federal institutions it had served, how concentrated those buyers were, and how concentrated its co-award partners were. v0.9.2 keeps v0.9.1's recipe but drops ten of its features, because they could not be rebuilt as of the contract date or would mark the data source: ad_period_days, amount_residual_z, industry_mismatch, has_partida, pub_delay_z, institution_diversity (replaced by its as-of version, inst_hhi_prior), co_bid_rate, price_hyp_confidence, institution_risk and amendment_flag. The chart shows the ElasticNet coefficients the system scores with, in each feature's own units (C=0.0037, l1_ratio=0.919, with T=0.530 folded in). Positive coefficients increase the risk indicator; negative coefficients decrease it.
features.footerNote: Coefficients from an ElasticNet tuned on an internal validation split (C=0.0037, l1_ratio=0.919), then multiplied by T=0.530 so the score is not steeper than the data support (ranking unchanged). One feature is regularized to exactly zero (yearEnd). Run: CAL-v92-asof-20261022.

riskEvidence.p1: Each risk factor is grounded in peer-reviewed literature on procurement corruption. The table below shows each factor's learned coefficient, global evidence strength, and key source. Hover over a factor name for mechanism details.

findings.finding1Body: In the units the system scores with, the largest weight is uneven contract sizes (+0.811: how much a vendor’s contract amounts swing against similar contracts in its sector), followed by prior buyer concentration (+0.771) and breadth (+0.592). Recency (−0.066) measures days since the vendor's previous contract with the same institution, so frequent repeat contracting raises the score. The weights are in each feature's own units, not standardised: they say how much the indicator rises per unit, not which feature matters most.
findings.finding2Title: Key changes from v0.9.1 to v0.9.2
findings.finding2Item1End: — Rebuilt from co-award partners in years before the contract only, the concentration of a vendor's partners now lowers the score.
findings.finding2Item2Strong: Buyer concentration before the contract now carries weight
findings.finding2Item2End: — At equal breadth, a vendor whose earlier sales were concentrated on few institutions scores higher. A vendor with no history counts as fully concentrated.
findings.finding2Item3End: — The single-award flag carries a small weight. Known-bad vendors tend to win through direct awards rather than single-award competitive procedures, so this classic OECD indicator adds little in Mexican federal procurement ground truth.
findings.finding3BodyStrong: The co-bid rate is not in v0.9.2
findings.finding3BodyEnd: — Its source table is missing, so the as-of rebuild dropped it; in v0.9.1 it was regularized to exactly zero. Co-bidding enters v0.9.2 only through the co-award Herfindahl, at −0.304.
findings.finding4Strong: In our case set, the classic indicators carry little weight
findings.finding4End: : single-award procedures, direct awards and short ad periods, which dominate international methodology (OECD, IMF), are weak or reversed here. The case set is small and skewed toward big scandals, so this is not enough to challenge those frameworks; it may reflect Mexican procurement or the limits of the sample.
findings.breadthTitle: Breadth: institutions served before the contract year (+0.592)
findings.breadthBody: One feature counts how many federal institutions a vendor had already sold to before the year of the contract, on a log scale, so each extra institution adds less. Among suppliers of similar size and age, those already selling to many agencies appear more often in documented cases, such as medicine and medical-equipment rings selling to dozens of IMSS and ISSSTE units. Going from three prior institutions to ten adds about +0.60 on the logit scale.
findings.breadthLimit: What it does not do: breadth works against the capture pattern. A vendor captured by one institution sells to few, so this feature lowers its score, even at equal size. The score is not built to catch single-institution capture, intermediaries or ghost companies; use the Capture view and the Red Flags patterns (P6 single-buyer dependence, P3 intermediary, P2 low footprint) for those.

validation.p1Start: RUBLI’s case set when the model was trained:
validation.p1Strong: 1,417 labelled cases (361 from press reports, 25 from official records, 1 audit report, 989 leads the model or ARIA surfaced and analysts wrote up, 41 other); today there are {{today}}
validation.p1End: . Most cases are analyst write-ups of model-surfaced leads, not adjudicated findings, and unlabelled contracts are treated as negatives even though some are surely corrupt. Case vendors are linked to their contracts within each case window.
validation.footnote: An earlier edition of this page showed a per-case detection table computed with the superseded v5.1 model, which leaked future information into training. It has been withdrawn. Per-case figures for vendors used in training would be in-sample; v0.9.2 reports its accuracy only on held-out case vendors, in years after its training data.
validation.lookAheadP1: The previous model (v0.9.1) used data from years after each contract. Several of its vendor features were computed over the vendor’s whole history, including the years that came after the contract being scored: scoring a 2019 contract, it could see that vendor’s data from 2020 onward. Nobody has that information at the time of contracting.
validation.lookAheadP2: We found it with a pre-registered test: the rules and thresholds were signed before the run, and it was run once. We rebuilt v0.9.1 with the same recipe but with vendor-history features that only look at earlier years, and tested both forward. At equal vendor size, the stored v0.9.1 scored AUC 0.906; rebuilt on the past only, 0.741. On vendors with no earlier history at all, the stored model scored 0.945, which a history-based indicator cannot earn honestly. Its edge came from future information, not skill.
validation.lookAheadP3: Since October 2026 the active indicator is v0.9.2: v0.9.1’s recipe over 17 features: each vendor’s history looks only at years before the contract; comparisons with its sector use the last three years, leaving the contract itself out. Its forward-chained AUC is 0.827 (95% CI 0.763 to 0.883); at equal vendor size, 0.741. A forward-chained AUC measures how often the model, trained only on earlier years, ranks a vendor with a documented case above one without a case in the following year. It is a different and harder test than the one behind the 0.852 published before; the two figures are not comparable. v0.9.2 also scores ComprasMX contracts.
validation.lookAheadP4: What it means for older readings: every v0.9.1 score (on this platform until October 2026, in ARIA memos, in stories citing v0.9.1 figures and in the 2026.10 Zenodo dataset) was computed with that future information. They stay on record but are superseded: do not quote them as current, and look up the v0.9.2 score.
validation.metricHighPlus: Hold-out case contracts scored high+ (out of sample)
validation.technicalNote: Forward test: for each year from 2019 to 2025, the model is fit on earlier years and scores that year. 174 vendor-years of held-out case vendors against vendor-years of held-out non-case vendors; paired vendor-cluster bootstrap, 1,000 resamples. AUC 0.827 (95% CI 0.763 to 0.883); at equal size 0.741 (0.687 to 0.794); on vendors with no earlier history, 0.741. The hyperparameters are v0.9.1’s own; nothing was tuned on this test. The test set had been looked at once before (pre-registration 1), which is disclosed. Not comparable with v0.9.1’s 0.852, which came from a different test.
validation.gateBBody: The conditions were signed before the test ran: the lower 95% bound of the forward AUC must be at least 0.65 (it is 0.763), and at equal size the model must beat the best rule without labels, ranking by the vendor’s earlier money (difference 95% CI +0.008 to +0.086). It passes both. The intercept is pinned so that 10% of contracts reach high or above, which fixes the scale by policy rather than by the data: the 0-to-1 value is not a probability.
validation.topPrecision: Top of the list: among the 100 highest-scored hold-out contracts, 62 belong to case vendors, against 78 for v0.8.5. Of v0.8.5's 78, 72 come from just three vendors that v0.8.5 very likely saw in training, so its lead there reflects that, not a better model. We disclose it anyway.
validation.fpNote: A score is computed from a contract's procurement features only; case labels are never read at scoring time. So a vendor whose link to a case was judged a false positive can still score critical on its own contract patterns, and the score says nothing about that case.

methods.zScoreP1: Each feature is compared with the same sector over the trailing three years [Y−2, Y], leaving the scored contract out of its own baseline; when the sector window has fewer than 30 rows, the national window is used. A direct award in a sector where most awards are direct is less unusual than in one where few are.
methods.zScoreFormula: z_i = (x_i - mu_i(sector, Y-2..Y, without the contract)) / sigma_i(sector, Y-2..Y, without the contract), clipped to ±5
methods.logisticP1: A single global ElasticNet logistic regression (C=0.0037, l1_ratio=0.919) trained on contracts of case vendors inside each case window, grouped by vendor. Sector differences enter through the sector-and-year z-score normalization of every feature, not through separate models.
methods.logisticNote: v0.9.2 uses the 17 v0.9.1 features that can be computed from the past only; the ElasticNet penalty drives one of them to exactly zero. On the forward test it scores AUC 0.827; at equal vendor size, 0.741.
methods.puP1Start: Since unlabeled contracts are not necessarily clean (some may be corrupt but undetected), we apply a Positive-Unlabeled learning correction:
methods.puNote: v0.9.2 uses c = 0.436 (Elkan & Noto). Scores are rescaled; the displayed score is compressed above 0.60 and never passes 0.95. IMPORTANT: The SCAR assumption is structurally violated — known cases are high-profile scandals and model-surfaced leads, not a random sample of all corruption.
methods.bootstrapP1: v0.9.2 does not publish per-contract confidence intervals; the intervals quoted on this page are for the model’s accuracy on the forward test (vendor-cluster bootstrap). Treat small differences between scores as noise.

v33section.p1End: with 8 base factors aligned to the IMF Corruption Risk Index methodology. Each factor contributed a percentage of the total score, with interaction bonuses for correlated factor pairs. Scores were preserved in the
v33section.bonusFactors: Additional bonus factors: Co-bidding +5%, Amount outlier +5%, Industry Mismatch +3%, Institution Risk +3%. 5 interaction pairs with up to +15% bonus. Score capped at 1.0.

dataSources.p1End: , the Mexican government's official electronic procurement system. CompraNet data spans 4 structures with varying column counts and quality levels; from 28 September 2025 the record continues with ComprasMX open data. A single-award procedure is a competitive procedure that ended with one winner: CompraNet records winners, not bidders, so RUBLI cannot say how many firms bid. Its rate is always stated over competitive procedures, never over all contracts.
dataSources.horizonBodyEnd: : CompraNet through 28 September 2025 (its federal bulk file; CompraNet was legally abolished in April 2025) and ComprasMX after that, up to the cut-off, with the open-data files of the platform that replaced it. 2026 is a partial year.
dataSources.horizonNote: The ComprasMX files run from 28 September 2025 to the cut-off ({{cut}}) and are refreshed every week. 93% come from federal agencies and the rest from states and municipalities spending federal money, as in CompraNet. Model v0.9.2 scores them like everything else, since all its inputs exist without looking ahead; «sin indicador» remains for contracts pending scoring and rejected amounts. We date contracts by start date so both sources are comparable. Official data contains errors: 15 contracts with decimal errors were corrected or excluded on 20 October 2026, and any contract above 100 billion pesos is rejected.
dataSources.gapsBody: COMPRANET publishes no annual contracts file for 2004. The register holds only 7 contracts dated that year (7.3 million pesos), against about 54,000 in 2003 and 57,000 in 2005. Treat 2004 as missing data, not a year of low spending, and leave it out of year-over-year comparisons.
dataSources.gapsPartialBody: CompraNet's federal bulk file froze on 28 September 2025 after it was abolished; from that date the year is completed by ComprasMX contracts.
dataSources.datingBody: Each contract is counted in the year of its contract date. Until 30 September 2026, 175,767 contracts published in COMPRANET's 2010 file but signed in 2011 (78,605) or 2012 (97,162), worth 320.6 billion pesos, were counted in 2010. That inflated 2010 and deflated 2011–2012. Because procedure type is only coded from the 2010 file onward, 2011 is the first year with comparable direct-award and single-award rates. 8,298 recent contracts that carry no contract date keep the year of the file they were published in.
dataSources.rejectEnd: Contracts exceeding 100B MXN are excluded as data entry errors (decimal point mistakes in original COMPRANET data).
dataSources.flagEnd: Contracts between 10B and 100B MXN are included but marked for manual review.
dataSources.context: Context: Mexico's entire federal budget is ~8T MXN annually. A 100B contract would be 1.25% of the national budget.

references.footer: Risk scores are statistical indicators, not verdicts. A high score indicates similarity to patterns in labelled cases -- it does not constitute proof of wrongdoing.

tiers.kicker: HOW TO INTERPRET FINDINGS · CONFIDENCE TIERS
tiers.intro: Not all RUBLI findings carry equal certainty. Every claim — whether in a risk score, an ARIA flag, or a story — belongs to one of three tiers. The tier determines the language you should use when citing or reporting it.
tiers.tierIBody: An independent authority — SAT, SFP, or a documented judicial process — has formally established fraud, simulated operations, or a procurement irregularity.
tiers.tierISource3: · Cases with an official source (25 of 1,417 at training; the rest are press-reported or analyst-labelled)
tiers.tierIIBody: Algorithmic risk signal plus at least one independent external source pointing in the same direction. Neither source alone is conclusive; together they warrant priority investigation.
tiers.tierIIEx1: · Critical risk score + EFOS Presunto match
tiers.tierIIIBodyStart: RUBLI's algorithm detected procurement characteristics that statistically resemble those of vendors linked to documented cases. No external source corroborates the flag.
tiers.tierIIIBodyStrong: Most RUBLI findings are Tier III.
tiers.tierIIIEx3: · Suppliers awarded together again and again (pattern P4)
tiers.tierIIISay: "statistical pattern consistent with" · "flagged for investigation" · "behavioral anomaly"
tiers.criticalRuleBody: Never use Tier I words («confirmed», «proven») for a Tier III finding. The risk indicator is not a verdict: it says where to look. A 0.90 means strong resemblance to documented cases. It is not a 90 % chance of guilt. A P2 (low-footprint) signal is detected by the algorithm; nobody has confirmed it.

limitations.intro: These limitations are inherent to the data sources, modeling approach, and legal constraints of the platform. Understanding them is essential to interpreting risk scores correctly.

dataLabels.riskMeaningCritical: Very close to vendors linked to documented cases
dataLabels.riskMeaningHigh: Close to vendors linked to documented cases
dataLabels.riskMeaningMedium: Moderately close to vendors linked to documented cases
dataLabels.riskMeaningLow: Far from vendors linked to documented cases
dataLabels.ariaModelCoefficients: Dot matrix showing model coefficient values by feature
dataLabels.ariaRiskFactorWeights: Dot matrix showing risk factor weights in the v3.3 model
dataLabels.structureE_desc: ComprasMX, since 28 September 2025. Every row carries an RFC.

limitationsTable.row2_i: Salud and Agricultura are over-represented (IMSS, Segalmex, DICONSA/LICONSA); cases with few contracts (La Estafa Maestra: 10, Grupo Higa: 3, Oceanografía: 2) are detected less; small-vendor and multi-sector corruption is underdetected
limitationsTable.row2_f: Add more labeled ground truth cases
limitationsTable.row3_i: 989 of today’s cases are leads the model or ARIA surfaced and analysts wrote up
limitationsTable.row3_f: Accuracy is reported only on held-out case vendors, in later years
limitationsTable.row4_i: With fewer than three prior contracts a vendor almost never reaches high: a «Low» there means insufficient history, not low risk
limitationsTable.row4_f: Read the score with the vendor’s record
limitationsTable.row5_i: Small-shell EFOS vendors still challenging to detect
limitationsTable.row6_f: Merged on RFC and exact name; doubtful pairs are not merged
limitationsTable.row7_l: Co-bidding: no signal of its own
limitationsTable.row7_i: co_bid_rate is not in v0.9.2 (its source table is missing); co-bidding enters only through the co-award Herfindahl (−0.304); bid rotation and cover bidding are not in the score
limitationsTable.row8_i: Its federal feed froze on 28 Sep 2025; later contracts come only from ComprasMX open data
limitationsTable.row9_i: 12% of records, the least reliable: structure A (2002–2010) has 0.1% RFC coverage; network analysis needs 2010+ data
limitationsTable.row10_i: A high score is a statistical anomaly consistent with documented patterns, not proof; it needs investigative follow-up
limitationsTable.row10_f: By design — the model informs, it does not conclude; establish facts with primary sources
limitationsTable.row12_i: New fraud patterns may be undetected
limitationsTable.row14_i: c=0.436 covers only scandal-similar corruption: known cases are high-profile scandals, not a random sample
limitationsTable.row14_f: Better labeled data from SAT, ASF
limitationsTable.row15_i: Since v0.9.2 every vendor feature looks only at years before the contract; v0.9.1 used the full history
limitationsTable.row16_i: Intercept −3.633 pinned so that about 10% of contracts reach high or above (inside the 2–15% target); the 0-to-1 value is not a probability
limitationsTable.row17_l: Red Flags tier 1 leans on known cases
limitationsTable.row17_i: Without an external record the priority indicator (IPS) cannot exceed 0.67, so tier 1 needs one, almost always a case link
limitationsTable.row17_f: Disclosed in «Red Flags: how the queue is ordered»
